read.sections.0.text.source:
Art can communicate authority, a recognised or claimed power to rule, through a ruler's image, an impressive setting, or objects worn on the body. Size, material, clothing and symbols can make status visible. Different societies connected art with political and religious life in different ways. A huge sculpture and a piece of jewellery offer two examples.

The Met's sphinx of Hatshepsut was made in ancient Egypt around 1473–1458 BCE. A lion's body supports the pharaoh's human head. The head wears a royal headcloth and a ceremonial false beard. Hatshepsut governed first as regent, someone who rules for another person, and then as senior co-ruler with Thutmose III. Her images followed established conventions, or usual ways, of showing a king. Yet some of her statues showed her as a woman.
read.sections.0.text.note: convention chosen as แบบแผน (easier than ขนบ / ขนบนิยม). Hatshepsut referred to as พระนาง and her father as พระบิดา, the usual school form for a queen; KEY_TERMS asks for plain royal words, so check this is not too much. Names of people (Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Thutmose I) kept in Latin letters per the brief. regent as ผู้สำเร็จราชการ. New Kingdom as สมัยอาณาจักรใหม่.
read.sections.0.text.back:
Art communicates authority, or power to govern that is accepted or claimed, through images of rulers, awe-inspiring places or things worn on the body. Size, materials, clothing and symbols make status visible. Different societies connect art with political and religious life in different ways. A large sculpture and a piece of ornament are two examples.

The Sphinx of Hatshepsut in the Metropolitan Museum of Art was made in ancient Egypt around 1473–1458 BCE. A lion's body supports the pharaoh's human head. The head wears the king's headcloth and a false beard used in ceremonies. Hatshepsut first ruled as regent, or one who rules in place of another, then ruled with Thutmose III as the senior ruler. Her images follow the convention, or usual way, of showing kings, but some statues show her as a woman.

She wears a royal head cloth and a false beard for ceremonies. First, Hatshepsut ruled for someone else. Then she ruled alongside Thutmose III, as the senior ruler. read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Art can show authority. Authority is the power to govern or lead others. Art may use pictures of rulers, grand places or things people wear. Size, materials, clothes and symbols can show a person's status. Each society links art and power in its own way.

The Sphinx of Hatshepsut comes from ancient Egypt, made around 1473 to 1458 BCE. It has a lion's body and a human head. The head is Hatshepsut, a pharaoh, or ruler of Egypt. She wears the king's headcloth and a false beard for ceremonies. At first Hatshepsut ruled in place of someone else. Later she ruled with Thutmose III as the more senior ruler. Her statues often follow the usual convention for showing kings, but some statues show her as a woman.

read.sections.1.text.source:
This granite sphinx was one of at least six at Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri, a temple linked with her burial and memory. The strong animal body, royal features and great size connected the ruler with strength. A group of sphinxes joined sculpture to architecture and royal memory. The museum's sphinx was rebuilt from pieces found by excavation. Its preservation is another part of its history.

This was a setting in Egypt's New Kingdom, not one timeless style of Egyptian government. At Hatshepsut's temple, the central sanctuary, or holiest room, belonged to Amun-Re, a major god worshipped at nearby Karnak. Spaces for offerings also honoured Hatshepsut and her father, Thutmose I. So religious ceremonies and the royal family were connected in the way the building was arranged. A ruler could show links with earlier kings while honouring a god. Such a display could claim legitimacy, the accepted right to rule, but it does not prove that everyone accepted it. The sphinx belonged to this setting of worship and kingship. It was not a portrait standing on its own.
read.sections.1.text.note: mortuary temple as วิหารสำหรับพิธีศพ (plain, avoids ราชาศัพท์ พระศพ). The god Amun-Re written in Thai as อามุน-รา (a god, not a person, so transliterated); Deir el-Bahri as เดียร์เอล-บาห์รี, Karnak as คาร์นัก. legitimacy as ความชอบธรรม; sanctuary as ห้องบูชาชั้นใน.
read.sections.1.text.back:
This granite sphinx is one of at least 6 sphinxes at Hatshepsut's funerary temple at Deir el-Bahri, a temple connected with her burial and remembrance. The strong animal body, royal features and huge size connect the ruler with strength. Sphinxes set in groups joined sculpture with architecture and the remembrance of the king. The museum's sphinx was reassembled from fragments found in excavation, so keeping it is another part of its history.

This is a place from Egypt's New Kingdom, not the one form of Egyptian rule that never changed. At Hatshepsut's temple, the central inner shrine, or most sacred room, belonged to Amun-Ra, a major god worshipped at nearby Karnak. Spaces for offerings also honoured Hatshepsut and her father, Thutmose I. So religious and royal ceremony were connected through the layout of the building. A ruler could show a link to earlier kings while honouring the gods. Such display could be used to claim legitimacy, or an accepted right to rule, but it does not prove everyone accepted it. The sphinx was part of this place of worship and kingship, not a portrait standing on its own.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
This stone sphinx stood at her temple at Deir el-Bahri. It was one of at least six. The temple was linked with her burial and memory. The lion body and royal face linked her with strength. Its great size did too. The museum's sphinx was found broken. It was put back together from pieces dug up from the ground.

This was in Egypt's New Kingdom period. The temple's holiest room was for Amun-Re, an important god. Other rooms honoured Hatshepsut and her father. So worship and the royal family were joined in one building. The ruler showed links with past kings. She also honoured a god. This could support her legitimacy. That means people accept a ruler's right to rule. But it does not prove that everyone did. The sphinx was part of this temple. It was not a picture standing alone.

The lion body and royal face link her with strength. So does the huge size. The museum's sphinx was found broken. It was put back together from pieces dug out of the ground.

This is from Egypt's New Kingdom. The temple's most sacred room belonged to Amun-Ra, a major god. Other rooms honoured Hatshepsut and her father. So worship and the royal family were together in one building. The ruler showed a link with past kings. She also honoured the gods. This might help support her legitimacy, meaning people accept a ruler's right to rule. But it does not prove everyone accepted it. The sphinx was part of this temple, not a picture standing alone.

read.sections.2.text.source:
Across the Atlantic, Moche artists on the north coast of present-day Peru made an ear ornament with a winged runner around 400–700 CE. Gold surrounds a mosaic of turquoise, sodalite and shell. A mosaic is a picture made from small pieces. Moche communities built regional centres, farmed coastal deserts and used the Pacific Ocean's resources. They shared practices without forming one central state. They lived centuries before the Inca. "Peru" tells us where they lived in today's terms; it does not name their ancient nation.

The ornament's tube-shaped back fitted through a stretched earlobe and held up the decorated front. Objects like this marked out high-status people through their materials, craftsmanship and display on the body. Evidence shows that powerful women as well as men wore ear ornaments. This kind of adornment made the body a place for showing social position. That is different from meeting a huge sculpture in a temple.

The runner holds a small bag, but the exact meaning of the image is uncertain. Museo Larco, a museum in Peru, links the varied stones and shells in Moche ear ornaments with trade over long distances by powerful people. Skilled makers combined materials as well as designing images. This linked display on the body to a wider supply of valued resources.

Comparing the two works does not make Egyptian and Moche institutions the same. It shows how particular artists turned materials into different public signs of power, and why their historical settings matter.
read.sections.2.text.note: Moche as โมเช (Mochica in the teachers' note as โมชิกา); adornment as เครื่องประดับกาย (glossary) to keep it apart from เครื่องประดับ (jewellery); mosaic as โมเสก (Royal Institute spelling). Museo Larco kept in Latin as an institution name. turquoise/sodalite as หินเทอร์ควอยซ์ / หินโซดาไลต์.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Across the Atlantic Ocean, Moche artists on the north coast of present-day Peru made an ear ornament shaped like a winged runner around 400–700 CE. Gold surrounds a mosaic of turquoise, sodalite and shell. A mosaic is a picture made of small pieces. Moche communities built regional centres, farmed the coastal desert and used resources from the Pacific Ocean. They shared practices without joining into one central state. They lived many centuries before the Inca. The word “Peru” tells us where they lived by today's name, not their ancient nation's name.

The back of the ornament is a tube-shaped rod that passes through a stretched earlobe and holds the decorated front. Objects like this showed who had high status through material, craftsmanship and being worn for others to see. Evidence shows that both powerful women and men wore ear ornaments. Body adornment like this made the body a place to display social status, unlike meeting a large sculpture in a temple.

The runner holds a small bag, but the exact meaning of the image is uncertain. Museo Larco, a museum in Peru, links the many kinds of stone and shell in Moche ear ornaments with long-distance trade by powerful people. Skilled makers did not only design the image but also brought materials together. This links display on the body with wider sources of valuable resources.

Comparing these two works doesn't make Egyptian and Moche institutions the same. It shows how each group of artists turned materials into different public symbols of power, and why a work's historical context matters.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Far away, in what is now Peru, Moche artists made an ear ornament. It is from about 400 to 700 CE. It shows a runner with wings. Gold goes around a mosaic. A mosaic is a picture made of small pieces. Here the pieces are blue and green stones and shell. Moche people built towns, farmed the desert and used the ocean. They shared ways of life. But they did not have one central government. They lived long before the Inca.

A tube on the back went through a stretched earlobe. Powerful people wore ornaments like this. Powerful women wore them too, not only men. This adornment showed a person's rank on their body. That is different from seeing a huge statue in a temple.

The runner holds a small bag. No one knows exactly what the picture means. A museum in Peru links the stones and shells with trade over long distances. Makers chose and joined these materials with skill.

The two works are very different. Both link art with power. But each belongs to its own place and time.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:

A mosaic is a picture made of small pieces. Here the pieces are blue stone, green stone and shell. The Moche built towns, farmed in the desert and used the ocean. They had a shared way of life but no single central government. They lived long before the Inca.

A tube at the back passes through a stretched earlobe. Powerful people wore ornaments like this. Powerful women wore them too, not only men. This body adornment shows a person's status on the body, unlike seeing a big statue in a temple.

The runner holds a small bag. No one knows for sure what the picture means. A museum in Peru links the stones and shells with long-distance trade. The makers chose and combined these materials with skill.

write.prompt.source: Pick the sphinx or the ear ornament. Explain how one feature helps show authority or status. Give one fact from its history, and say which part of your answer is an interpretation. Two or three sentences are enough.
write.prompt.back: Choose the sphinx or the ear ornament. Explain how one feature helps show authority or status, give one fact from the work's history, and say which part of your answer is interpretation. 2 or 3 sentences is enough.

write.example.source: One feature of the sphinx is its lion's body with Hatshepsut's head and royal headcloth. A fact from its history is that it was one of at least six sphinxes at her temple, where a god and the royal family were honoured. My interpretation is that the strong lion body and the temple setting were meant to link her with strength and the gods. This does not prove that everyone accepted her rule.
write.example.back: One feature of the sphinx is the lion's body with Hatshepsut's head and the king's headcloth. A fact from the work's history is that it was one of at least 6 sphinxes at her temple, a place honouring gods and the royal family. My interpretation is that the strong lion body and the temple setting were meant to link her with strength and the gods. This does not prove everyone accepted her rule.
